text: Cheeky Pint Oct 12, 2026 3 2 Share As Meta scales its AI infrastructure past five gigawatts, Mark Zuckerberg (founder and CEO, Meta) and Alexandr Wang (Chief AI Officer, Meta Superintelligence Labs) join John for a pint to discuss the launch of Muse Wonder and the future of personal AI agents. In this episode, Mark and Alex open up about the creation of Meta Superintelligence Labs (MSL), the decision to execute a complete talent reboot, and what it really feels like to make a $100B+ CapEx commitment before knowing if the model will work. They dive deep into the architecture of Muse Wonder—including active memory, multimodal perception, and frontier coding—while laying out their vision for agentic commerce, hardware form factors like smart glasses, and why superintelligence belongs in the hands of billions. John Collison Yes. Mark Zuckerberg And I’m constantly telling it like, all right... Like, look you took 30 seconds to give me that feedback. I only have a 60-second break. Like, you gotta go faster. Just optimize yourself, optimize yourself. And it’s, I think, a good example of how stuff is going to go in the future where basically everyone is actually going to be writing tons of code. They’re just not going to know that they’re writing code. John Collison What kind of MMA steers does a model give you? Mark Zuckerberg Um, you want to see? John Collison Yeah. Mark Zuckerberg Basically, let me see if I can pull some stuff out. But basically it gives me a lot of stuff about balance and, like, hip position. I’ll pull up some stuff. You guys should try this. Alexandr Wang It was definitely one of his first use cases actually of even the initial prototypes. John Collison Yeah. Yeah. Mark Zuckerberg I mean, I did this with OpenClaw before we even had Muse working. It was just like... Then that’s why I was saying it’s kind of like become an eval for this too. Alexandr Wang It’s good. I actually didn’t know that it was an eval for the product. So noted. Mark Zuckerberg Yeah. There you go. John Collison How is all this... In the model’s training data, like the fine-grained, this is what an MMA fighter looks like when they’re appropriately balanced, and this is when they’re like too much on the back foot. Just, I’m wondering, how has it consumed so many images of appropriate versus inappropriate MMA posture? Mark Zuckerberg Here you can see it. It just pulls out frames from it and it’s like too much on my back leg there. John Collison Yeah, but is this the emergent intelligence? Like it does actually... Mark Zuckerberg So, I mean, I think that that’s like kind of making good multimodal models. So like the question is why would Meta want to build these models? Mark Zuckerberg First of all, I think just superintelligence overall is going to allow us to run the company better and build all kinds of different things. But for the products that we’re building, there’s certain capabilities and certain mixes of skills that basically are just much more applicable to these cases. So I mean, this is one of the things that Alex focused on from the beginning was like, all right, we really want to make sure that our multimodal program is good because that’s disproportionately important for the types of things that people use all these services for. John Collison How do you train a good multimodal model? John Collison Is this where Meta just has an advantage because you guys have so much image and video data? Mark Zuckerberg It’s very helpful. Alexandr Wang Yeah. And I think ultimately, a lot of this, it comes down to how are you focused on it, right? I think because of the fact that we wanted to build personal superintelligence. And fundamentally, I think most people in the world really experience the world in a highly multimodal way. They like talking to other people and listening to things and seeing videos and filming things of their own. I think most consumers have this highly multimodal experience. And especially earlier this year, there was actually a point of tension almost in the industry because I think so much of the consensus view within the AI industry was that it was just all about coding and coding was all that mattered. And I think that for the success of a product like Muse and the success of a lot of these consumer use cases, it really depends on the ability to be strong and multimodal. Mark Zuckerberg Yeah. So even the text-based interaction model, I think it’s something that people do. I mean, everyone texts. It’s like you can let it hear what you are listening to, and it can talk to you, and it can see what you see if you let it. And then eventually, I don’t even know if we’re going to have an app store on the glasses. It’ll just be like a multimodal generation that kind of creates whatever you need right in your vision. But for now, the perception work has been really impressive. John Collison I want to ask you guys about the product space here in AI and try something out on you. Then we have to talk about stablecoins. Like, it would take me a long time. But somehow there’s a very small number of clearly correct products in AI as opposed to it being this, like, very broad and complicated product space. Mark Zuckerberg I kind of disagree. John Collison Sure. Every company has one of those. I mean, ours is Meta AI. It reaches a ton of people, but I mean, it’s like the same thing that all these companies have. John Collison It’s retrieval, not delegation or something. Mark Zuckerberg Yeah, and even like when you say it has a computer... Yeah, but there’s lots of different ways to do that, right? Alexandr Wang It’s kind of like how when mobile first started happening, it was like, “Oh, it’s just an app and everything is just an app.” Well, it turns out there’s a lot of nuance in what exactly an app is. John Collison Okay. So you guys think I’m making the classic mistake, which is like, my domain is complex and this domain is, again, from a product point-of-view, it’s simple. Alexandr Wang So it’s aware of its memory as a core system. John Collison Okay. Alexandr Wang And then when faced with various setbacks along the way, the ability to identify other solutions to those problems in an aligned way. John Collison Okay. John Collison Yes. Mark Zuckerberg And we hope to, you know, at some point not too far from now, have a model that is as good as Wonder, but in the Spark form factor. Alexandr Wang Empirically by the benchmarks, one would conclude that. Mark Zuckerberg Yes. John Collison I see. Mark Zuckerberg Yes. John Collison Yeah, people inside companies like complaining about Goodhart’s Law. You know, a metric that becomes a target ceases to become a good metric.
